request.system:
You are the requirements analyst in a governed software delivery pipeline. You turn a product owner's requirement into a normalized engineering specification that the architect, coders and testers downstream will build from. You do not write code.

Your output is checked by automated gates and then reviewed by a human before any design or code work starts, so precision matters more than polish.

How to work:
- Restate the goal in one or two sentences an engineer could act on.
- List functional and non-functional requirements as atomic, testable statements. Keep the requirement's own ids (FR1, NFR2, ...) when it provides them; otherwise assign them. Do not invent scope the requirement does not ask for.
- Surface every ambiguity: anything an engineer would have to guess about (formats, limits, error behaviour, status codes, security posture). Include the requirement's own "open points" and any you find yourself.
- For each ambiguity, decide whether a safe, conventional default exists.
  - If it does, set `source` to "assumption", put the default in `resolution`, and explain in `rationale` why it is the conventional and low-risk choice. These become recorded decisions a human will review.
  - If the answer is a genuine product decision (who may see data, business rules, legal or compliance posture, anything where a wrong guess would be costly to reverse), set `source` to "unresolved" and `resolution` to null. This stops the pipeline until a human answers, which is the intended behaviour. Do not guess on these to keep things moving.
- Write acceptance criteria as observable behaviours (request → expected response), covering the main path and the important failure paths.
- `summary`: one line, e.g. counts of requirements and how many ambiguities were resolved vs. left open.

<requirement>
# Requirement: URL Shortener Service (v1, greenfield)

> Input to the orchestrator. Written as a product owner would: intentionally
> mostly-specified, with a few open points the Analyst agent must surface.

## Goal
Provide an HTTP service that turns long URLs into short, shareable links and
redirects visitors from the short link to the original URL.

## Functional requirements
- FR1 Create a short link for a long URL. Optionally accept a custom alias.
- FR2 Optionally accept an expiry; expired links must stop redirecting.
- FR3 Visiting a short link redirects to the original URL.
- FR4 Fetch metadata for a short link (original URL, created, expiry).
- FR5 Delete a short link.
- FR6 Health endpoint for operations.

## Non-functional requirements
- NFR1 Redirect path is latency-sensitive (target p99 < 50 ms in-process).
- NFR2 Only `http`/`https` URLs are accepted; reject obviously malicious or
  internal-network targets.
- NFR3 Protect the create endpoint from abuse.
- NFR4 Runs locally with a single command; no external infrastructure.
- NFR5 Automated tests with meaningful coverage.

## Known open points (for the Analyst to resolve or flag)
- Short-code length / alphabet not specified.
- Redirect status code (301 vs 302) not specified.
- Behaviour when a custom alias is already taken.
- Rate-limit thresholds not specified.
</requirement>

Make the requirements and acceptance criteria consistent with every answer. Raise a new open question only if an answer itself leaves something genuinely undecided.

acceptance_criteria: POST /api/links with a valid HTTP or HTTPS URL and no alias or expiry returns 201 and includes a generated 8-character code, relative shortUrl, createdAt, null expiresAt, and a managementToken.
POST /api/links with a valid custom alias and future RFC 3339 expiry returns 201; the returned link uses that alias and the returned expiry is normalized to UTC.

POST /api/links with an alias outside the permitted length or alphabet, or with a reserved path name, returns 400. Repeating a case-sensitive alias already in use returns 409 and leaves the existing link unchanged.
POST /api/links with a URL longer than 2,048 characters, a non-HTTP(S) scheme, localhost, or a host resolving to a prohibited address returns 400 and creates no link.
POST /api/links with an unresolvable destination hostname returns 400 and creates no link.

GET /{code} for an active link returns 302 with a Location header equal to the original URL. GET /{code} for an expired link returns 410 and does not redirect; for an unknown or deleted link it returns 404.
GET /api/links/{code} without credentials returns 200 with originalUrl, createdAt, and expiresAt for an existing link, including an expired one. It returns 404 for an unknown or deleted link.

DELETE /api/links/{code} with the matching X-Management-Token returns 204; subsequent redirect and metadata requests for that code return 404. A missing or invalid token returns 401 and does not delete the link.
After a service restart, a previously created link remains available and its metadata is unchanged; the in-memory creation-rate limit is reset.
After a client IP exceeds 20 create-endpoint requests in a minute, a subsequent request from that IP returns 429 with Retry-After. A request from a different client IP is limited independently.
GET /health returns 200 when the service and H2 persistence are available and 503 when required persistence is unavailable.

The automated in-process redirect test performs 1,000 requests after warm-up from a single client on the local machine and asserts p99 latency below 50 ms; results are documented as indicative, not as a production SLO.

ambiguities.question: What characters, length limits, and case-sensitivity rules apply to custom aliases?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision defines the custom-alias syntax, matching behavior, and reserved names used by FR1 and NFR2.
ambiguities.resolution: Custom aliases are 3-32 characters from [A-Za-z0-9_-], case-sensitive (consistent with generated codes). Reserved words are rejected: api, health, links (and any path the service itself uses).

ambiguities.question: What rate limit applies to link creation, over what interval, and how are clients identified (for example, by IP address)?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision supplies the threshold, interval, client key, response, limiter storage, and restart behavior for NFR3.
ambiguities.resolution: 20 link creations per minute per client IP address. Exceeding it returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. Limits are held in memory (Bucket4j); a restart resets them.

ambiguities.question: Who is allowed to fetch metadata or delete a link, and is authentication or authorization required?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision defines metadata visibility, deletion authorization, the v1 account scope, and token storage for FR1, FR4, and FR5.
ambiguities.resolution: Metadata (GET) is public. Creating a link returns a one-time management token; DELETE requires that token (e.g. an X-Management-Token header), so only the creator can delete. No user accounts in v1. Store only a hash of the token, never the token itself.

ambiguities.question: Must links survive service restarts, and where should local link data be stored?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision defines persistence and migration requirements for NFR4.
ambiguities.resolution: Yes, links must survive restarts. Use file-based H2 under ./data with Flyway-managed schema migrations.

ambiguities.question: Precisely which destinations count as malicious or internal, and should validation cover DNS-resolved addresses, IPv4, IPv6, and address changes over time?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision defines the accepted schemes, length limit, prohibited destinations, validation timing, and DNS-repointing limitation for NFR2.
ambiguities.resolution: Accept only http/https URLs up to 2048 characters. Reject localhost and any host that is, or resolves to, a loopback, private, link-local, unique-local or multicast address (IPv4 and IPv6), checked once at creation. Re-pointing DNS after creation is an accepted, documented limitation: the service never fetches the URL.

ambiguities.question: What traffic volume, concurrency, measurement window, and runtime conditions define the p99 latency target?
ambiguities.rationale: Decided by a human: This binding decision defines the test conditions and status of the latency target in NFR1.
ambiguities.resolution: Measured in-process by an automated test: 1,000 redirect requests after a warm-up, single client, local machine, asserting p99 < 50 ms. Documented as an indicative check, not a production SLO.

ambiguities.question: What length and alphabet should generated short codes use?
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement leaves generated-code length and alphabet open. Eight characters is a conventional compact code length, and using the explicitly accepted alias alphabet and case sensitivity keeps lookup behavior consistent. Generate codes randomly and retry on collision.
ambiguities.resolution: Generate unique, case-sensitive 8-character codes from [A-Za-z0-9_-], using the same alphabet as custom aliases.

ambiguities.question: Which redirect status code should be used?
ambiguities.rationale: A temporary redirect is a conventional, low-risk choice for links that may expire or be deleted; it avoids clients permanently caching a destination.

ambiguities.question: What happens when a requested custom alias is already in use?
ambiguities.rationale: 409 Conflict is the conventional response for a uniqueness conflict and prevents an alias request from changing an existing link.
ambiguities.resolution: Reject the creation with 409 Conflict; do not overwrite the existing link.

ambiguities.question: Which HTTP routes, JSON field names, and success/error response formats should the service expose?
ambiguities.rationale: The requirement specifies HTTP capabilities but no wire contract. A small REST-style route set, JSON fields, relative short path, and conventional status codes provide a simple local contract without requiring a public hostname.
ambiguities.resolution: Use POST /api/links to create, GET /{code} to redirect, GET /api/links/{code} for metadata, DELETE /api/links/{code} for deletion, and GET /health for health. Create accepts JSON fields url and optional alias and expiresAt. Create returns 201 with code, shortUrl (the relative path /{code}), createdAt, expiresAt, and managementToken. Metadata returns originalUrl, createdAt, and expiresAt. Use 200 for metadata, 204 for successful deletion, and JSON error bodies with error and message fields. Format timestamps as RFC 3339 UTC. Use 400 for invalid input, 401 for a missing or invalid management token, and 404 for an unknown or deleted code.

ambiguities.question: What expiry timestamp format and exact boundary behavior should be used, and what should metadata return for an expired link?
ambiguities.rationale: RFC 3339 is a conventional interoperable timestamp format. Treating expiry as exclusive at the specified instant makes the boundary testable; 410 conventionally indicates a resource that is no longer available, while retaining metadata is consistent with FR4 and does not permit redirecting.
ambiguities.resolution: Accept RFC 3339 timestamps with an offset and normalize them to UTC. Reject malformed timestamps and timestamps not later than creation with 400. A link is expired at current time >= expiresAt; return 410 Gone for an expired-link redirect. Continue returning public metadata for expired links until deletion.

ambiguities.question: How should management tokens be generated and hashed?
ambiguities.rationale: A cryptographically random 256-bit secret and one-way hash are conventional, low-risk defaults for a bearer management credential and implement the human decision to store only a hash.
ambiguities.resolution: Generate each token from 32 cryptographically random bytes, encode it as unpadded base64url, and store a SHA-256 hash for comparison. Return the raw token only in the successful create response; it remains valid for the creator's subsequent DELETE request until the link is deleted.

ambiguities.question: What should happen if DNS resolution fails during destination validation?
ambiguities.rationale: Failing closed is a conventional security default for a required internal-address check; accepting an unchecked hostname could bypass the binding destination restrictions.
ambiguities.resolution: Fail closed: reject the URL at creation if its hostname cannot be resolved or the DNS check cannot complete.

ambiguities.question: What response should the health endpoint provide, and what does healthy mean?
ambiguities.rationale: A simple readiness-style health check that includes the service's required local persistence is a conventional operational default and matches FR6 without adding external dependencies.
ambiguities.resolution: Return 200 when the service can serve requests and its H2 persistence is available; otherwise return 503. Use GET /health.

ambiguities.question: How should the IP-based limiter handle requests behind proxies, and do invalid create attempts count toward the limit?
ambiguities.rationale: Using the peer address avoids trusting spoofable forwarding headers by default. Counting all create-endpoint attempts is a conventional abuse-control policy that prevents invalid requests from bypassing the limiter.
ambiguities.resolution: Key the limiter by the direct network peer IP and ignore forwarded-IP headers unless trusted-proxy handling is explicitly configured. Count every request reaching POST /api/links, including invalid attempts.

ambiguities.question: After deletion, may a short code or custom alias be reused for a new link?
ambiguities.rationale: Reusing a deleted code can cause an old shared URL to lead to a different destination; permanently reserving it requires a different storage policy. Neither the requirement nor the clarifications specify which behavior is desired, and a wrong choice could create user or security surprises.

functional.text: Create a short link from a submitted URL, optionally using a custom alias. Apply the URL and alias validation rules in NFR2 and the recorded API contract. On success, return the short link and a management token that is displayed only in the create response.
Optionally accept an expiry timestamp. Reject malformed or non-future expiry values. A link is expired when the current time is at or after its expiry, and an expired link must not redirect.
A request to a short-link code redirects to its original URL while the link is active. Expired, unknown, and deleted links do not redirect.
Provide public metadata for a short link, including its original URL, creation timestamp, and expiry (null when none is set). Metadata remains available for an expired link until it is deleted.

Delete a short link only when the request includes its valid management token in the X-Management-Token header. A successful deletion makes the link unavailable for redirect and metadata lookup. Do not store the token itself; store only its hash.
Provide an operations health endpoint that reports whether the service and its local persistence can serve requests.

data.goal: Provide a locally runnable HTTP service that creates short links for valid HTTP/HTTPS URLs and redirects visitors to their destinations. The service also supports expiry, public metadata, creator-authorized deletion, and an operations health endpoint.

non_functional.text: Meet the indicative in-process redirect latency target: p99 under 50 ms in an automated test of 1,000 redirect requests after warm-up, from a single client on the local machine. This is not a production SLO.

Accept only HTTP and HTTPS URLs up to 2,048 characters. Reject localhost and hosts that are, or resolve to, loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, or multicast IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. Perform this check once at creation; do not fetch the destination URL. DNS changes after creation are an accepted, documented limitation. Custom aliases must be 3–32 characters from [A-Za-z0-9_-], case-sensitive; reject reserved words api, health, links, and any path used by the service.

Limit link-creation requests to 20 per minute per client IP using an in-memory Bucket4j limiter. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when the limit is exceeded. A service restart resets the limits.
Run locally with one documented command and no external infrastructure. Persist links in file-based H2 under ./data and manage schema migrations with Flyway; links must survive service restarts.

Provide automated tests with meaningful coverage of the functional requirements and important failure paths, including validation, expiry, authorization, rate limiting, persistence across restart, and the redirect latency check.

data.summary: 11 requirements; 16 ambiguities: 15 recorded assumptions and 1 unresolved product decision.
